newsitem.title: UK: BT shareholders meet to vote on MCI deal.
newsitem.headline: BT shareholders meet to vote on MCI deal.

text.p: British Telecommunications Plc shareholders met on Tuesday to vote on the company's ambitious $20 billion merger with MCI Communications Corp, America's second-largest long distance telecoms carrier.

Shareholders meeting in London's Wembley Conference Centre were expected to vote in favour of the deal, largest transatlantic merger in history, which will create Concert Plc -- one of the world's biggest telecoms giants.

"I have reservations about the merger but I know so little. I am not always sure that bigger is better," said Stella Garton-Brown, a pensioner who has held a few hundred BT shares since its privatisation in 1984.

MCI shareholders approved the merger in the U.S. two weeks ago and analysts on this side of the Atlantic had expected a similar welcome here -- especially as a transatlantic road show by the two companies last month sent BT's shares surging.

Although some analysts warn that a 30 percent premium that BT is paying for the 80 percent of MCI it did not already own is a high price to pay for control, the powerful financial institutions, that own about 73-74 percent of BT, tend traditionally to back company boards.
As an added incentive, the proposed merger has been sweetened with a 2.2 billion pound special dividend for BT shareholders.
The deal will create the world's fourth largest telecoms group in terms of sales after Japan's Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp (NTT), America's AT&T and Germany's Deutsche Telekom.

Concert wants to provide clients around the globe with local, long distance, international and mobile phone services as well as multi-media, Internet-based services and systems integration for business clients.

The group plans to be represented in key countries across the world so it can focus on winning high-margin, multinational clients that analysts estimate account for about 15-20 percent of global telecoms revenue.

BT has made much of what it calls the "tremendous growth prospects" of the venture. The United States is the world's largest telecoms market. It is also home to 40 percent of the world's largest multinational company headquarters -- some of the most valuable customers for global telecoms alliances.
One hurdle still standing in Concert's way is regulatory clearance in Europe and the U.S.
"Companies, like people, reach critical stages in their lives...we have reached that stage," said BT Chairman Sir Iain Vallance.
Of the 620,000 shareholders voting by proxy, 99 percent approved the merger, BT said.
